questions.question: Why do React developers often use `map()` when rendering data?
options: Because `map()` changes CSS styles automatically
Because `map()` turns each item in an array into a new value, often a JSX element
Because `map()` is required for all React components
Because `map()` stores state for each list item
questions.explanation: In React, `map()` is commonly used to transform an array of data into an array of JSX elements for rendering.

questions.question: Why is a `key` prop usually added when rendering a list with `map()`?
options: Because `key` makes the text bold by default
Because React uses `key` to track list items more reliably when rendering updates
Because `map()` does not work without `key` in JavaScript
Because `key` is how components receive props
questions.explanation: When rendering lists, React uses `key` to identify items more reliably across renders. A stable key helps React update the UI correctly.

questions.question: What usually happens if you render a list with `map()` but do not include a `key` prop on the repeated elements?
options: React will always crash immediately
The list will never appear on the page
React will usually show a warning and list updates may become harder for React to track correctly
JavaScript will automatically add keys for you using the variable name
questions.explanation: If list items do not have a `key`, React will usually show a warning. The UI may still render, but React has a harder time tracking which items changed between renders.
